claim: Basal skin cells in zebrafish larvae are sensitive to changes in osmolarity after wounding.
source: We find that, in addition to sensing osmolarity, basal skin cells in zebrafish larvae are also sensitive to changes in the particular ionic composition of their surroundings after wounding, specifically the concentration of sodium chloride in the immediate vicinity of the wound.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: Basal skin cells in zebrafish larvae are sensitive to changes in the concentration of sodium chloride in the immediate vicinity of the wound.
source: We find that, in addition to sensing osmolarity, basal skin cells in zebrafish larvae are also sensitive to changes in the particular ionic composition of their surroundings after wounding, specifically the concentration of sodium chloride in the immediate vicinity of the wound.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: The sodium chloride-specific wound detection mechanism is independent of cell swelling.
source: This sodium chloride-specific wound detection mechanism is independent of cell swelling, and instead is suggestive of a mechanism by which cells sense changes in the transepithelial electrical potential generated by the transport of sodium and chloride ions across the skin.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: Electric fields directly applied within the skin are sufficient to initiate actin polarization of basal cells in vivo.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we show that electric fields directly applied within the skin are sufficient to initiate actin polarization and migration of basal cells in their native epithelial context in vivo, even overriding endogenous wound signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: Electric fields directly applied within the skin are sufficient to initiate migration of basal cells in vivo.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we show that electric fields directly applied within the skin are sufficient to initiate actin polarization and migration of basal cells in their native epithelial context in vivo, even overriding endogenous wound signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: Electric fields can override endogenous wound signaling in basal cells in vivo.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we show that electric fields directly applied within the skin are sufficient to initiate actin polarization and migration of basal cells in their native epithelial context in vivo, even overriding endogenous wound signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: Skin cells respond to both osmotic and electrical perturbations arising from tissue injury to mount a robust wound response.
source: This suggests that, in order to mount a robust wound response, skin cells respond to both osmotic and electrical perturbations arising from tissue injury.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion of the study.

claim: The initial wound response in many tissues consists of rearrangements of the actomyosin cytoskeleton to form a contractile purse string.
source: The initial wound response in many tissues consists of rearrangements of the actomyosin cytoskeleton to form a contractile purse string that closes the wound in concert with protrusive actin structures that promote cell migration toward the injury and help cover the damaged area (Abreu-Blanco et al., 2012; Eming et al., 2014; Rothenberg and Fernandez-Gonzalez, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The initial wound response in many tissues includes protrusive actin structures that promote cell migration toward the injury.
source: The initial wound response in many tissues consists of rearrangements of the actomyosin cytoskeleton to form a contractile purse string that closes the wound in concert with protrusive actin structures that promote cell migration toward the injury and help cover the damaged area (Abreu-Blanco et al., 2012; Eming et al., 2014; Rothenberg and Fernandez-Gonzalez, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Waves of calcium influx occur in cells hundreds of microns away from a wound less than a minute after injury.
source: Yet many internal signaling events—including waves of calcium influx, hydrogen peroxide release, and purinergic signaling—occur in cells hundreds of microns away from a wound less than a minute after injury, suggesting that there must be other mechanisms by which cells sense injury on a tissue-wide scale (Niethammer et al., 2009; Razzell et al., 2013; Xu and Chisholm, 2011; Yin et al., 2007; Yoo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Hydrogen peroxide release occurs in cells hundreds of microns away from a wound less than a minute after injury.
source: Yet many internal signaling events—including waves of calcium influx, hydrogen peroxide release, and purinergic signaling—occur in cells hundreds of microns away from a wound less than a minute after injury, suggesting that there must be other mechanisms by which cells sense injury on a tissue-wide scale (Niethammer et al., 2009; Razzell et al., 2013; Xu and Chisholm, 2011; Yin et al., 2007; Yoo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Purinergic signaling occurs in cells hundreds of microns away from a wound less than a minute after injury.
source: Yet many internal signaling events—including waves of calcium influx, hydrogen peroxide release, and purinergic signaling—occur in cells hundreds of microns away from a wound less than a minute after injury, suggesting that there must be other mechanisms by which cells sense injury on a tissue-wide scale (Niethammer et al., 2009; Razzell et al., 2013; Xu and Chisholm, 2011; Yin et al., 2007; Yoo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Interstitial fluid in saltwater fishes is hyposmotic relative to the environment.
source: This ion transport maintains the distinct composition and osmolarity of interstitial fluid relative to the surrounding environment: for example, interstitial fluid in saltwater fishes is hyposmotic relative to the environment, while in freshwater fishes it is hyperosmotic (Boisen et al., 2003; Potts, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Interstitial fluid in freshwater fishes is hyperosmotic relative to the environment.
source: This ion transport maintains the distinct composition and osmolarity of interstitial fluid relative to the surrounding environment: for example, interstitial fluid in saltwater fishes is hyposmotic relative to the environment, while in freshwater fishes it is hyperosmotic (Boisen et al., 2003; Potts, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ion substitution and pharmacological inhibition of ion channels suggests that transport of sodium and chloride ions is essential for maintaining the TEP in different tissues.
source: Ion substitution and pharmacological inhibition of ion channels suggests that transport of sodium and chloride ions is essential for maintaining the TEP in different tissues (Dietz et al., 1967; McCaig and Robinson, 1982; Reid et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The wound response in Xenopus laevis larvae is inhibited when the composition of the external medium resembles that of interstitial fluid.
source: In Xenopus laevis (clawed frog) and Danio rerio (zebrafish) larvae, the wound response is inhibited when the composition of the external medium resembles that of interstitial fluid (Fuchigami et al., 2011; Gault et al., 2014), but this observation alone cannot distinguish between osmotic and electrical mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The wound response in Danio rerio larvae is inhibited when the composition of the external medium resembles that of interstitial fluid.
source: In Xenopus laevis (clawed frog) and Danio rerio (zebrafish) larvae, the wound response is inhibited when the composition of the external medium resembles that of interstitial fluid (Fuchigami et al., 2011; Gault et al., 2014), but this observation alone cannot distinguish between osmotic and electrical mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cell swelling due to osmotic shock following injury provides a physical, cell-autonomous cue of tissue damage in zebrafish epidermal cells.
source: Regarding osmotic cues, in zebrafish epidermal cells, cell swelling due to osmotic shock following injury has been shown to provide a physical, cell-autonomous cue of tissue damage, and this cue is amplified and relayed to other cells with subsequent extracellular ATP release (Gault et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Osmotic swelling is amplified and relayed to other cells with subsequent extracellular ATP release in zebrafish epidermal cells.
source: Regarding osmotic cues, in zebrafish epidermal cells, cell swelling due to osmotic shock following injury has been shown to provide a physical, cell-autonomous cue of tissue damage, and this cue is amplified and relayed to other cells with subsequent extracellular ATP release (Gault et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Hypotonic shock can promote formation of lamellipodia.
source: In addition to promoting signaling at the tissue level, osmotic swelling could also mechanically promote migration at the cellular level: hypotonic shock can promote formation of lamellipodia (Chen et al., 2019) and can intrinsically stabilize a polarized actin cytoskeleton by increasing mechanical feedback through membrane tension (Houk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Hypotonic shock can intrinsically stabilize a polarized actin cytoskeleton by increasing mechanical feedback through membrane tension.
source: In addition to promoting signaling at the tissue level, osmotic swelling could also mechanically promote migration at the cellular level: hypotonic shock can promote formation of lamellipodia (Chen et al., 2019) and can intrinsically stabilize a polarized actin cytoskeleton by increasing mechanical feedback through membrane tension (Houk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Electric currents have been directly measured emanating from wounds in adult zebrafish skin within the first few hours after injury.
source: Electric currents have been directly measured emanating from wounds in many animal tissues in this early phase, including adult zebrafish skin, rat cornea and skin, tails of newt and Xenopus tadpoles, bronchial epithelia of rhesus macaques, and even human skin (Ferreira et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2009; Li et al., 2012; Nawata, 2001; Reid et al., 2009; Reid et al., 2007; Reid et al., 2005; Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

source: Electric currents have been directly measured emanating from wounds in many animal tissues in this early phase, including adult zebrafish skin, rat cornea and skin, tails of newt and Xenopus tadpoles, bronchial epithelia of rhesus macaques, and even human skin (Ferreira et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2009; Li et al., 2012; Nawata, 2001; Reid et al., 2009; Reid et al., 2007; Reid et al., 2005; Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

source: Electric currents have been directly measured emanating from wounds in many animal tissues in this early phase, including adult zebrafish skin, rat cornea and skin, tails of newt and Xenopus tadpoles, bronchial epithelia of rhesus macaques, and even human skin (Ferreira et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2009; Li et al., 2012; Nawata, 2001; Reid et al., 2009; Reid et al., 2007; Reid et al., 2005; Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The currents measured emanating from wounds are approximately 10-100 times stronger than regeneration or developmental currents in the same model systems.
source: The currents measured emanating from these wounds are ~10–100 times stronger than regeneration or developmental currents in the same model systems (Ferreira et al., 2016; Reid et al., 2005; Robinson, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In rat cornea, pharmacological perturbations that increase the magnitude of the wound current also correspondingly increase the rate of wound closure.
source: In rat cornea, pharmacological perturbations that increase or decrease the magnitude of the wound current also correspondingly increase or decrease the rate of wound closure, suggesting that electrical currents may aid in healing (Reid et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In rat cornea, pharmacological perturbations that decrease the magnitude of the wound current also correspondingly decrease the rate of wound closure.
source: In rat cornea, pharmacological perturbations that increase or decrease the magnitude of the wound current also correspondingly increase or decrease the rate of wound closure, suggesting that electrical currents may aid in healing (Reid et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A wide variety of cell types migrate directionally in the presence of an electric field.
source: The response of cultured cells to applied electric fields has been better studied than responses in vivo, and it has been observed that a wide variety of cell types migrate directionally in the presence of an electric field (Allen et al., 2013; Riding and Pullar, 2016; Sun et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most cells appear to be responsive to the current density in their surroundings rather than the magnitude of the electric field per se.
source: Importantly, most cells appear to be responsive not to the magnitude of the electric field per se (in V/cm), but rather to the current density in their surroundings (in mA/cm2), which is directly proportional to the electric field, scaled by the conductivity of the medium (Allen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A prevailing model is that electric fields drag charged membrane proteins to one side of the cell by electrophoresis, with the resulting asymmetric protein distribution leading to cytoskeletal polarization.
source: The signaling networks that allow cells to respond to electric fields are still being unraveled, but a prevailing model is that electric fields drag charged membrane proteins to one side of the cell by electrophoresis, with the resulting asymmetric protein distribution leading to cytoskeletal polarization, mediated by key signal transduction factors including phosphoinositide-3-kinase (PI3K) (Allen et al., 2013; Sarkar et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cells respond almost immediately (within seconds or minutes) to electric fields applied in culture.
source: Intriguingly, cells respond almost immediately (within seconds or minutes) to electric fields applied in culture, raising the possibility that they could also be responsive to the electric fields generated immediately after wounding in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The zebrafish larval epidermis is bilayered, with a superficial cell layer and a basal cell layer.
source: The zebrafish larval epidermis is bilayered, with a superficial cell layer originating from the enveloping layer in early embryogenesis, and a basal cell layer that resides on a collagenous basal lamina and is specified by the ∆Np63 promoter (Bakkers et al., 2002; Le Guellec et al., 2004; Rasmussen et al., 2015; Sonawane et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: External culture medium for zebrafish has an osmolarity of about 10 mOsmol/l.
source: Because zebrafish are freshwater organisms, the osmotic gradient across the zebrafish epidermis is large: external culture medium has an osmolarity of about 10 mOsmol/l while the osmolarity of interstitial fluid inside the fish is estimated to be about 270–300 mOsmol/l (Boisen et al., 2003; Gault et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The osmolarity of interstitial fluid inside zebrafish is estimated to be about 270-300 mOsmol/l.
source: Because zebrafish are freshwater organisms, the osmotic gradient across the zebrafish epidermis is large: external culture medium has an osmolarity of about 10 mOsmol/l while the osmolarity of interstitial fluid inside the fish is estimated to be about 270–300 mOsmol/l (Boisen et al., 2003; Gault et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: At least five types of ionocytes are responsible for maintaining ion homeostasis in zebrafish.
source: At least five types of ionocytes are responsible for maintaining ion homeostasis in zebrafish, each with a distinct complement of ion pumps, channels, and transporters, coupled by distinct electrochemical gradients (Guh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Within seconds after injury, the basal cell layer reacts to tissue damage primarily by active cell migration.
source: Previous work in zebrafish has shown that, within seconds after injury, the basal cell layer reacts to tissue damage primarily by active cell migration while the superficial layer reacts by purse string contraction around the wound (Gault et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Within seconds after injury, the superficial layer reacts by purse string contraction around the wound.
source: Previous work in zebrafish has shown that, within seconds after injury, the basal cell layer reacts to tissue damage primarily by active cell migration while the superficial layer reacts by purse string contraction around the wound (Gault et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Lacerated tissue rapidly reorganized and contracted around the wound site over a period of about 15-20 min.
source: We found that lacerated tissue rapidly reorganized and contracted around the wound site over a period of about 15–20 min (Figure 1B), consistent with wound closure observed with other methods mentioned above.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Laceration wounds induce a more pronounced migratory response within the first few minutes after wounding compared to tail transection.
source: In timelapse videos of wounds from both techniques, laceration wounds induce a more pronounced migratory response within the first few minutes after wounding, suggesting that laceration wounds may be ideal for studying the early stages of the wound response (Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments and shown in Figure 1—video 1.

claim: Within two minutes of injury, actin polarized with significant accumulation of LifeAct-labeled filamentous structures on the wound-facing edges of the cell.
source: Within two minutes of injury, actin polarized with significant accumulation of LifeAct-labeled filamentous structures on the wound-facing edges of the cell, and the formerly static cell boundary began to rapidly protrude and retract on a sub-minute timescale, reminiscent of actin ruffling (Figure 1C; Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments and shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—video 2.

claim: The formerly static cell boundary began to rapidly protrude and retract on a sub-minute timescale within two minutes of injury.
source: Within two minutes of injury, actin polarized with significant accumulation of LifeAct-labeled filamentous structures on the wound-facing edges of the cell, and the formerly static cell boundary began to rapidly protrude and retract on a sub-minute timescale, reminiscent of actin ruffling (Figure 1C; Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments and shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—video 2.

claim: For cells close to the wound, dynamic actin-rich ruffles stabilized into lamellipodial sheets that protruded rapidly, causing the cells to elongate and translocate parallel to their long axis.
source: For cells close to the wound, these dynamic actin-rich ruffles stabilized into lamellipodial sheets that protruded rapidly, causing the cells to elongate and translocate parallel to their long axis.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: Isolated migratory basal epidermal cells typically adopt a wider, 'canoe-shaped' morphology and move perpendicular to their long axis.
source: This differs from the behavior of these cells when isolated in culture, where they have been studied extensively for their rapid and persistent migration and are often referred to as keratocytes (Lou et al., 2015). Isolated migratory basal epidermal cells typically adopt a wider, 'canoe-shaped' morphology and move perpendicular to their long axis with protrusions that maintain a persistent shape during migration (Keren et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The polarized actin ruffling response and cell elongation toward the direction of the wound was apparent for basal cells up to several hundred micrometers away.
source: In vivo, the polarized actin ruffling response and cell elongation toward the direction of the wound was apparent for basal cells up to several hundred micrometers away, although these distant cells typically did not physically translocate (Figure 1—video 3).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments and shown in Figure 1—video 3.

claim: Distant cells typically did not physically translocate after injury.
source: In vivo, the polarized actin ruffling response and cell elongation toward the direction of the wound was apparent for basal cells up to several hundred micrometers away, although these distant cells typically did not physically translocate (Figure 1—video 3).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments and shown in Figure 1—video 3.

claim: The migratory phase of the wound response process was rapid, with cells polarizing, migrating, and stopping within about 15-20 min after injury.
source: The migratory phase of the wound response process was rapid, with cells polarizing, migrating, and stopping within about 15–20 min after injury.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: Laceration prompted a stronger cell migration response within the first 5 min of injury compared with tail transection.
source: Interestingly, laceration prompted a stronger cell migration response within the first 5 min of injury compared with tail transection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)—perhaps due to mechanical differences between the two methods, such as the increased tissue stretch applied with the laceration wound—and the profile of cell speed in space and time was reproducible across larvae despite the variation in the shapes of the laceration-induced wound margins as compared to other wounding protocols (Figure 1E, line graphs).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Laceration induced intense and rapid propagation of increased calcium levels throughout the tailfin.
source: Consistent with observations from other model systems and wounding methods, we found intense and rapid propagation of increased calcium levels throughout the tailfin (Figure 1F; Figure 1—video 4).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments and shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—video 4.

claim: The calcium wave propagated about five times faster than the cell migration wave (200 µm/min vs. 40 µm/min).
source: This calcium wave propagated about five times faster than the cell migration wave (200 µm/min vs. 40 µm/min, Figure 1G), implying that there is no uniform time delay between the calcium transient in a cell and the onset of migration.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: There is no uniform time delay between the calcium transient in a cell and the onset of migration.
source: This calcium wave propagated about five times faster than the cell migration wave (200 µm/min vs. 40 µm/min, Figure 1G), implying that there is no uniform time delay between the calcium transient in a cell and the onset of migration.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the calcium wave propagates much faster than the cell migration wave.

claim: Cell movement is not directly triggered or regulated by the increase in calcium.
source: The same trend is observed when directly comparing the average changes in cell migratory speed and in GCaMP6f fluorescence intensity over time, normalized to comparable dimensionless quantities, where the change in GCaMP6f intensity is much faster than the change in cell speed (Figure 1H). This suggests that cell movement is not directly triggered or regulated by the increase in calcium, though calcium may indirectly promote wound-induced migration by functioning as a permissive cue.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the change in GCaMP6f intensity is much faster than the change in cell speed, as shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Calcium may indirectly promote wound-induced migration by functioning as a permissive cue.
source: The same trend is observed when directly comparing the average changes in cell migratory speed and in GCaMP6f fluorescence intensity over time, normalized to comparable dimensionless quantities, where the change in GCaMP6f intensity is much faster than the change in cell speed (Figure 1H). This suggests that cell movement is not directly triggered or regulated by the increase in calcium, though calcium may indirectly promote wound-induced migration by functioning as a permissive cue.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that the change in GCaMP6f intensity is much faster than the change in cell speed, as shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Larvae wounded in isosmotic sodium chloride had a markedly reduced wound response compared to larvae in E3 (hypotonic treatment).
source: Larvae wounded in isosmotic sodium chloride had a markedly reduced wound response compared to larvae in E3 (hypotonic treatment), as measured by average basal cell speed over time (Figure 2A, compare red with black trace).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Although all isosmotic treatments did reduce average cell speed, sodium chloride had a uniquely strong inhibitory effect.
source: We found that, although all isosmotic treatments did reduce average cell speed, sodium chloride had a uniquely strong inhibitory effect (Figure 2A, compare red with other traces; Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments and shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—video 1.

claim: The degree to which all other osmolytes inhibited a wound response was remarkably consistent with each other.
source: In contrast, the degree to which all other osmolytes inhibited a wound response was remarkably consistent with each other (Figure 2A, compare all other traces).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The difference in magnitudes of the first principal component between sodium chloride treatment and all other treatments was statistically significant (p<0.001).
source: The difference in magnitudes of the first principal component between sodium chloride treatment and all other treatments was statistically significant (p<0.001, one-way fixed-effects Welch's ANOVA F(6, 19)=130.9, with Games-Powell post-hoc tests), while the differences among the other isosmotic treatments were not statistically significant (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated as a result of statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The differences among the other isosmotic treatments were not statistically significant.
source: The difference in magnitudes of the first principal component between sodium chloride treatment and all other treatments was statistically significant (p<0.001, one-way fixed-effects Welch's ANOVA F(6, 19)=130.9, with Games-Powell post-hoc tests), while the differences among the other isosmotic treatments were not statistically significant (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated as a result of statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: With the exception of the immediate vicinity around the wound, there was a striking lack of cytoskeletal reorganization in response to wounding in isosmotic sodium chloride.
source: Looking more closely at the dynamics of the cytoskeleton in the basal cell layer, we noticed that—with the exception of the immediate vicinity around the wound—there was a striking lack of cytoskeletal reorganization in response to wounding in isosmotic sodium chloride (Figure 2C; Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments and shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—video 1.

claim: In all other isosmotic treatment conditions, transient polarization of the actin cytoskeleton in cells from the basal layer was observed.
source: In contrast, in all other isosmotic treatment conditions we observed transient polarization of the actin cytoskeleton in cells from the basal layer (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: LifeAct intensity increased in all isosmotic treatments except sodium chloride.
source: This analysis revealed that LifeAct intensity increased (often due to formation of lamellipodia) in all isosmotic treatments except sodium chloride, which did not induce any measurable cytoskeletal response at equivalent positions relative to the wound (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Sodium chloride did not induce any measurable cytoskeletal response at equivalent positions relative to the wound.
source: This analysis revealed that LifeAct intensity increased (often due to formation of lamellipodia) in all isosmotic treatments except sodium chloride, which did not induce any measurable cytoskeletal response at equivalent positions relative to the wound (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Sodium chloride's non-osmotic effect on the wound response is associated with inhibiting cytoskeletal polarization.
source: This indicates that sodium chloride's non-osmotic effect on the wound response is associated with inhibiting cytoskeletal polarization.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that sodium chloride did not induce any measurable cytoskeletal response.

claim: The wound response in larvae immobilized by alpha-bungarotoxin in isosmotic sodium chloride was nearly identical to the response of larvae treated with Tricaine.
source: Larvae treated with this alternative inhibitor were not fully immobilized, presumably due to mRNA degradation at 3 dpf, but even so the wound response in larvae immobilized by alpha-bungarotoxin in isosmotic sodium chloride was nearly identical to the response of larvae treated with Tricaine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), suggesting the specific inhibitory effect of sodium chloride on the wound response is independent of the anesthetic used in the experiments.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The specific inhibitory effect of sodium chloride on the wound response is independent of the anesthetic used in the experiments.
source: Larvae treated with this alternative inhibitor were not fully immobilized, presumably due to mRNA degradation at 3 dpf, but even so the wound response in larvae immobilized by alpha-bungarotoxin in isosmotic sodium chloride was nearly identical to the response of larvae treated with Tricaine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), suggesting the specific inhibitory effect of sodium chloride on the wound response is independent of the anesthetic used in the experiments.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the wound response in larvae immobilized by alpha-bungarotoxin in isosmotic sodium chloride was nearly identical to the response of larvae treated with Tricaine, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The unique effect of sodium chloride on the wound response is not due to small differences in osmotic strength between solutions with different ionic composition.
source: Our findings are also robust to small variations in osmolarity: when solutions were deliberately prepared deviating from each other in osmolarity by 10% we found qualitatively similar responses in terms of migration and actin polarization (data not shown). This suggests that the unique effect of sodium chloride on the wound response is not due to small differences in osmotic strength between solutions with different ionic composition, but rather due to the actual chemical identities of the ions in solution.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that solutions deviating from each other in osmolarity by 10% produced qualitatively similar responses.

claim: The unique effect of sodium chloride on the wound response is due to the actual chemical identities of the ions in solution.
source: Our findings are also robust to small variations in osmolarity: when solutions were deliberately prepared deviating from each other in osmolarity by 10% we found qualitatively similar responses in terms of migration and actin polarization (data not shown). This suggests that the unique effect of sodium chloride on the wound response is not due to small differences in osmotic strength between solutions with different ionic composition, but rather due to the actual chemical identities of the ions in solution.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that solutions deviating from each other in osmolarity by 10% produced qualitatively similar responses.

claim: When isosmotic sodium chloride media was present on only the tailfin, the wound response was identical to when the entire larva was immersed in that media.
source: When the same media was present in both chambers of the device, cell movement in response to a wound was similar to the uniform incubation conditions. When isosmotic sodium chloride media was present on only the tailfin, the wound response was identical to when the entire larva was immersed in that media (Figure 2G, compare red and pink traces).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments and shown in Figure 2G.

claim: When hyposmotic media was present only on the tailfin, the wound response was similar to that observed with uniformly applied hyposmotic media.

claim: Cells situated between the two electrodes rapidly polarized their actin cytoskeletons and migrated in the direction of the cathode.

claim: Epidermal cells detect tissue injury through changes in their external ionic environment in at least two distinct ways.
source: Our results suggest that there are at least two distinct ways in which epidermal cells detect tissue injury through changes in their external ionic environment.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion of the study.

claim: Mixing of interstitial fluid with dilute external media causes cells to swell, which prompts a migratory response.
source: First, mixing of interstitial fluid with dilute external media causes cells to swell, which prompts a migratory response, as has been previously shown (Enyedi et al., 2016; Gault et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion of the study and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Fluid mixing specifically reduces the concentration of sodium and chloride ions around cells, which is sufficient to prompt actin polarization in basal epidermal cells near wounds, independent of cell swelling or any change in environmental osmolarity.
source: Second, this fluid mixing specifically reduces the concentration of sodium and chloride ions around cells, which we demonstrated is sufficient to prompt actin polarization in basal epidermal cells near wounds, independent of cell swelling or any change in environmental osmolarity.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion of the study.

claim: One mechanism for cells to detect wounds that would be consistent with the osmolarity-independent effect of sodium chloride is through direct detection of electric fields arising from ion transport across the epidermis.
source: One mechanism for cells to detect wounds that would be consistent with this osmolarity-independent effect of sodium chloride is through direct detection of electric fields arising from ion transport across the epidermis.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion of the study.

claim: Sodium and chloride are the predominant ions in both the interstitial fluids and external environments of freshwater fishes.
source: Sodium and chloride are the predominant ions in both the interstitial fluids and external environments of freshwater fishes, and these ions must be actively and continually absorbed from the environment to counteract leakage through tight junctions and urine (Kirschner, 2004; Potts, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sodium and chloride ions must be actively and continually absorbed from the environment to counteract leakage through tight junctions and urine in freshwater fishes.
source: Sodium and chloride are the predominant ions in both the interstitial fluids and external environments of freshwater fishes, and these ions must be actively and continually absorbed from the environment to counteract leakage through tight junctions and urine (Kirschner, 2004; Potts, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Transport of sodium and chloride ions may be partially interdependent but are ultimately distinct.
source: While transport mechanisms for these ions vary across species and environmental conditions, a consistent theme is that transport of sodium and chloride ions may be partially interdependent but are ultimately distinct: for example, the sodium-potassium ATPase can pump sodium ions against their concentration gradients, while chloride ions can be exchanged for bicarbonate ions, the concentration of which is regulated by the actions of carbonic anhydrase and V-ATPase proton pumps that expel excess protons (Guh et al., 2015; Kirschner, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The activity of various pumps and transporters can lead to charge separation across the epithelium, which manifests as the TEP.
source: The activity of these various pumps and transporters can lead to charge separation across the epithelium, which manifests as the TEP.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on established knowledge.

claim: TEPs have been measured in a variety of freshwater fish species, including trout, goldfish, and killifish, as well as in freshwater invertebrates like crayfish.
source: TEPs have been measured in a variety of freshwater fish species, including trout, goldfish, and killifish, as well as in freshwater invertebrates like crayfish (Eddy, 1975; Kerstetter et al., 1970; McWilliams and Potts, 1978; Wood and Grosell, 2008; Zare and Greenaway, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Differential permeability of fish skin to sodium versus chloride would lead to differing transport rates of these ions across the skin, resulting in a 'diffusion potential,' which could alter the TEP depending on the concentration of sodium and chloride in the external medium.
source: For example, it has been proposed that differential permeability of fish skin to sodium versus chloride would lead to differing transport rates of these ions across the skin, resulting in a so-called 'diffusion potential,' which could alter the TEP depending on the concentration of sodium and chloride in the external medium (Eddy, 1975; McWilliams and Potts, 1978; Potts, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sodium and chloride transport would have a particularly strong influence on the TEP.
source: Such a mechanism suggests that sodium and chloride transport would have a particularly strong influence on the TEP.
evidence: This is inferred from the proposed mechanism of differential permeability.

claim: When the skin is breached, the established TEP will be short-circuited, leading to electrical potential gradients within the skin, which generate electric fields whose orientation will depend on the relative position of the wound.
source: And as shown in Figure 4A, when the skin is breached, the established TEP will be short-circuited, leading to electrical potential gradients within the skin, which generate electric fields whose orientation will depend on the relative position of the wound (Reid and Zhao, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on established knowledge and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The transport of sodium and chloride ions has been empirically shown to be essential for TEP maintenance in rat cornea and amphibian epidermis.
source: Supporting this theoretical rationale for the specific relationship between sodium and chloride transport and the TEP in fish epidermis, the transport of these two ions has been empirically shown to be essential for TEP maintenance other tissues, including rat cornea and amphibian epidermis (Dietz et al., 1967; McCaig et al., 2005; Reid et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: An electric field is sufficient to direct cell movement in vivo in the absence of other wound cues.
source: In light of this plausible connection between electrical signaling and sodium chloride ion transport in fish skin, we have shown that an electric field is sufficient to direct cell movement in vivo in the absence of other wound cues, and can even override endogenous wound cues at the same timescale as the normal wound response.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion of the study.

claim: Electric fields can override endogenous wound cues at the same timescale as the normal wound response.
source: In light of this plausible connection between electrical signaling and sodium chloride ion transport in fish skin, we have shown that an electric field is sufficient to direct cell movement in vivo in the absence of other wound cues, and can even override endogenous wound cues at the same timescale as the normal wound response.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion of the study.

claim: The early wound currents fall in the range of 5-500 µA/cm2, three orders of magnitude lower than the applied currents that cultured cells can respond to.
source: Paradoxically, these early wound currents fall in the range of 5–500 µA/cm2, three orders of magnitude lower than the applied currents that cultured cells can respond to Allen et al., 2013; Cohen et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2011.
evidence: This is stated as an observation and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The most parsimonious explanation for the discrepancy between measured wound currents and applied currents that cultured cells can respond to is that the physiological currents to which cells respond in vivo are restricted to small intercellular spaces.
source: We believe that the most parsimonious explanation for this discrepancy is that the physiological currents to which cells respond in vivo are restricted to small intercellular spaces, so the effective cross-sectional area through which current passes is small, and the current density within those spaces is large (Robinson and Messerli, 2003).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: When currents leave the tissue, they spread over a much larger area, and so the current density measured just outside of a wound will be much smaller than the current density inside the tissue, which cells are actually sensing.

claim: Teleosts do not have a homolog to the amiloride-sensitive sodium channel implicated in establishing the TEP in frog skin.
source: Furthermore, traditional pharmacological approaches to dissecting ion transport mechanisms have had mixed success in zebrafish; for example, teleosts do not have a homolog to the amiloride-sensitive sodium channel implicated in establishing the TEP in frog skin, and the channel responsible for sodium uptake from the external environment remains unknown (Venkatesh et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Treatment of larvae with isotonic KCl elicited a similar wound response to other non-NaCl osmolytes, despite the strong effect KCl generally has on transmembrane potential.
source: At the cellular level, how might epidermal cells sense electric fields? Our results argue against a model in which this is accomplished primarily through changes in transmembrane potential: treatment of larvae with isotonic KCl elicited a similar wound response to other non-NaCl osmolytes, despite the strong effect KCl generally has on transmembrane potential (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In culture, basal epidermal skin cells from fish respond to electric fields through an electrophoretic mechanism, in which an unidentified membrane-bound protein (or proteins) is dragged by electrophoresis to one side of the cell, promoting cytoskeletal polarization and initiation or redirection of motility through a primary PI3K-dependent pathway and secondary myosin II-dependent pathway.
source: In culture, basal epidermal skin cells from fish respond to electric fields through an electrophoretic mechanism, in which an unidentified membrane-bound protein (or proteins) is dragged by electrophoresis to one side of the cell, promoting cytoskeletal polarization and initiation or redirection of motility through a primary PI3K-dependent pathway and secondary myosin II-dependent pathway (Allen et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A similar electrophoretic mechanism is suspected to be at work for the same cell type in zebrafish in vivo.
source: We suspect a similar mechanism is at work for the same cell type in zebrafish in vivo, and the electrophoretic mechanism is compatible with a model in which electric fields flow around cells within the epidermis immediately after wounding.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the results.

claim: Calcium dynamics are not required for sensing electric fields in cultured fish basal cells.
source: Although calcium dynamics are not required for sensing electric fields in cultured fish basal cells (Allen et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2009), it is possible this signaling mechanism may be more relevant within intact tissue in vivo, where large calcium transients are observed immediately following injury (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Electric fields are an attractive physical cue for wound detection because they are intrinsically directional.
source: Electric fields are an attractive physical cue for wound detection because they are intrinsically directional, providing a mechanism to rapidly coordinate cell migration toward a wound at the spatial scales of tissue.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Changes in osmolarity and cell swelling do not encode directional information.
source: In contrast, changes in osmolarity and cell swelling do not encode directional information; these cues can initiate a wound response but must be coupled with an additional spatial cue in order to orient cell movement appropriately.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Electric currents have been measured emanating from wounds in human skin.
source: Electric currents have been measured emanating from wounds in human skin, and human skin and nasal epithelium both maintain a TEP, suggesting that electric fields may be relevant for wound healing in humans (Foulds and Barker, 1983; Knowles et al., 1981; Reid et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Human skin and nasal epithelium both maintain a TEP.
source: Electric currents have been measured emanating from wounds in human skin, and human skin and nasal epithelium both maintain a TEP, suggesting that electric fields may be relevant for wound healing in humans (Foulds and Barker, 1983; Knowles et al., 1981; Reid et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Electric fields may be relevant for wound healing in humans.
source: Electric currents have been measured emanating from wounds in human skin, and human skin and nasal epithelium both maintain a TEP, suggesting that electric fields may be relevant for wound healing in humans (Foulds and Barker, 1983; Knowles et al., 1981; Reid et al., 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that electric currents have been measured emanating from wounds in human skin and that human skin and nasal epithelium both maintain a TEP.

claim: Zebrafish are an ideal model system to further interrogate how cells respond to electric fields in physiological contexts.
source: Our direct observation of actin polarization in response to electric fields in vivo at rapid timescales of 5–10 min bridges the gap between detailed mechanistic studies in cell culture and functional studies in tissues, and suggests that zebrafish are an ideal model system to further interrogate how cells respond to electric fields in physiological contexts.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion of the study.
